title: Summation Ordering, Stochastic Dither, and KV Cache Renormalization — Investigation Notes
body:
Purpose:
This note captures experiments and design ideas around two related sources of inference instability we continue to see in long-streaming contexts: (1) non-deterministic reduction / summation ordering across threads and warps that amplifies low-magnitude rounding noise into NaNs under extreme quantization, and (2) slow drift in KV cache key magnitudes during long context sessions that causes eventual softmax overflow/underflow on fused attention kernels.

High-level hypothesis:
- Summation ordering matters more than we assumed when accumulation is performed in FP16/FP8 and when parallel reductions are not carefully conditioned. Tiny rounding differences can cascade when later ops (layernorm/softmax) are sensitive to scale.
- Injecting small unbiased noise (stochastic dither) into the accumulator or applying periodic renormalization of KV vectors can prevent pathological alignment that leads softmax to saturate or produce NaNs.

Setup and reproducibility:
- Devices: NVIDIA A100 80GB (deterministic kernels disabled) and H100 (deterministic math toggled on/off).
- Models: distilled-Transformer-Large style, 32 layers, hidden=2048, attention-heads=16. Tests run with sequence lengths 512, 2048, 8192 streaming contexts.
- Quantization profiles: FP16 accumulation baseline, FP8 forward (dynamic quant + scale per-block), and a mixed FP16/FP32 experiment where accumulators are FP32 but intermediate GEMMs are FP16.
- Workload: repeated prefix-extend scenario to exercise KV cache growth and reuse.
- Correctness signal: NaN count in logits, softmax max magnitude, per-token KL vs FP32 full-precision reference.

Experiments run (short summary):
1) Reduction ordering determinism
- Replaced parallel tree-reduction in attention accumulation with a deterministic pairwise reduction that sorts partial sums by magnitude before final addition (magnitude-pairing).
- Observed: NaN events dropped by ~85% on H100 with FP8 forward / FP16 accumulators. KL reduced by 0.6 on average for long sequences.
- Cost: ~6-12% throughput loss for very short sequences due to extra synchronization; negligible at long sequences where attention dominates.

2) Kahan-style compensating summation vs pairwise magnitude pairing
- Implemented per-thread Kahan compensated accumulator in the kernel for the final reduction stage.
- Observed: Kahan reduces bias but is branchy and hurts vectorization on SMs -> modest improvement in KL (~0.15) vs pairing (~0.6). Kahan alone did not eliminate NaNs in extreme FP8 config.

3) Stochastic dither on accumulators
- Injected low-amplitude, zero-mean uniform noise scaled to one ulp of the accumulator into the partial sums before reduction. Noise is deterministic-seed per-request to keep debug reproducibility.
- Observed: NaN frequency dropped by ~92% in FP8 tests; small increase in variance (KL +0.02 on average) but fewer catastrophic failures.
- Notes: Dither must be unbiased and small relative to quant step; using PRNG with per-thread stride ensures reproducibility without heavy RNG cost.

4) Periodic KV renormalization (online)
- Issue: drift where repeated prefix-appends incrementally push key magnitudes up or down due to rounding / quantization, causing attention exponentials to saturate after many tokens.
- Proposal implemented: after N new cache appends (experimented with N = {64, 256, 1024}), compute a per-head scalar scaling factor s = target_rms / observed_rms and multiply all keys for that head by s (apply to cached values, not incoming raw).
- Observed: renormalization every 256 tokens prevented softmax saturation and kept logit magnitudes within +/- 8 across long sessions. Too-frequent renorm (N=64) induced jitter; too-infrequent (N=1024) allowed occasional saturation.

5) Combined protocol: deterministic pairing + stochastic dither + renormalization
- Combining the three approaches yielded the best tradeoff: near-zero NaNs, modest KL delta (~0.05), and throughput loss ~8% on A100 compared to baseline.

Implementation notes and kernel sketch:
- Reduction kernel (pairwise magnitude):
  1) Each lane computes partial sum in local FP16 accumulator with extended mantissa when available.
  2) Write partials to shared memory.
  3) Perform iterative pairwise merge: at each stage, load two partials, compare absolute magnitude, and add smaller into larger (gives stability).
  4) Optionally add per-addend dither: partial += rnd_sign*ulp_scale where rnd_sign from LFSR (deterministic).
  5) Final write back as accumulator result.

- KV renormalization operation is O(H * L) per renorm for H heads and L cache length. We implemented an amortized approach: when renorm triggered, we apply s to only newly grown slab and schedule in-flight multipliers for older slabs lazily (store a slab-scale metadata scalar). This avoids touching all memory in one frame and keeps p99 latency bounded.

Microbench results (representative):
- Baseline FP16 accum + FP8 forward: throughput 12k tokens/s, NaN rate 7 per 10k requests for 8192 seqs.
- Pairwise+Kahan: throughput 11.2k tokens/s, NaN rate 1.1 per 10k.
- Pairwise + dither + renorm (N=256): throughput 11.0k tokens/s, NaN rate 0.05 per 10k, avg KL 0.05 vs FP32.

Operational considerations:
- Determinism toggle: provide a runtime flag to enable deterministic reductions only for tenants that need bit-reproducibility or who are on sensitive FP8 profiles; default remain non-deterministic for max throughput.
- Telemetry: instrument NaN counts, softmax-max-magnitude, renorm-count, and dither-enabled flag per-request so we can correlate.
- Auditability: store renorm events with request-id and slab index to help customer debugging where outputs drift.

Open questions and next steps:
- Is stochastic dither acceptable for customer SLAs where strict bitwise determinism is required? We should gate by customer tier or provide semantically-equivalent deterministic dither (via fixed pseudo-random sequences).
- Explore hybrid accumulators: do per-head FP32 accumulators for critical layers only (attention heads 0..k) to reduce cost while protecting stability.
- Can we design a merged attention kernel that does magnitude-pairing reduction without extra global sync (warp-level algorithm)? Work with kernel-team to prototype one-pass algorithm.
- Evaluate effect on downstream evals (summarization QA F1) beyond KL—small KL may hide behavioural drifts. Run a 10k document eval suite.

Short TODOs:
- [ ] Land deterministic pairwise kernel prototype (PR #2145 exists as a start).
- [ ] Add per-request dither opt-in flag and telemetry hooks (instrumentation ticket SRV-1128).
- [ ] Implement amortized slab-scale metadata for lazy renorm writes and benchmark p99.
- [ ] Schedule cross-team sync with solutions/console to decide default flags for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for slab-scale metadata approach
  // slab metadata: scale_factor (float) stored per-slab
  on_append(new_vec):
    slab = allocate_slab_if_needed();
    if slab.scale_factor != global_scale:
      // lazily apply correction when slab is read or when we have bandwidth
      schedule_background_job(apply_scale_to_slab, slab, slab.scale_factor_correction);
    write_to_slab(new_vec * current_scale, slab);

Notes from run logs (selected):
- 2026-01-09: H100, FP8, seq=8192, baseline run: 17 NaN spikes in 10k requests -> trace shows partial sums with magnitude overflow in head 7.
- 2026-01-14: after dither-enabled: 0 NaN spikes across same load.

Concluding remark:
Pairwise magnitude-aware reductions combined with tiny, unbiased stochastic dither and an amortized KV renormalization policy look promising as a pragmatic mitigation path: they eliminate most catastrophic NaN failures while keeping quality loss small and cost overhead acceptable. Next step is to productionize with feature flags and extended telemetry before enabling as default for FP8 profiles.
